subject: Chemistry
title: Scheele's Green: Arsenic Wallpaper
description: One-minute skill: Scheele's Green: Arsenic Wallpaper.

hook.text: In the 1800s, green wallpaper was slowly killing families. The pigment was copper arsenite—laced with arsenic.

buildup.text: Scheele's Green was a vivid, cheap pigment made by reacting copper sulfate with arsenic trioxide.

discovery.text: In damp conditions, mold on the wallpaper converted the arsenic into toxic gas. Residents inhaled poison nightly.

twist.text: Napoleon may have been slowly poisoned by his green wallpaper on St. Helena. Hair samples show high arsenic levels.

climax.text: Even after the danger was known, green arsenic paint was used on children's toys and candy wrappers for decades.

punchline.text: A beautiful green pigment that released arsenic gas. Fashion literally killed.

quiz.question: How did arsenic green wallpaper poison people?
options: Mold on damp wallpaper converted arsenic into toxic gas that was inhaled
The green color itself damaged people's eyesight
Arsenic leaked through walls and contaminated drinking water

details.summary: Scheele's Green, copper arsenite, was a vivid green pigment used extensively in Victorian wallpaper, fabrics, and food coloring. In damp conditions, mold converted the arsenic compound to toxic trimethylarsine gas, slowly poisoning inhabitants of decorated rooms.
details.whyItMatters: Arsenic wallpaper poisoning may have affected thousands of Victorians including possibly Napoleon Bonaparte on St. Helena. The scandal drove early consumer product safety regulations.
takeaways: Scheele's Green contains copper arsenite that produces vivid green
Damp conditions enabled mold to release arsenic gas from wallpaper
The discovery helped establish consumer product safety legislation

faq.question: Could arsenic wallpaper have contributed to Napoleon's death in exile?
faq.answer: Hair samples from Napoleon show elevated arsenic levels, and his rooms on St. Helena had green wallpaper. However, deliberate poisoning, medicinal arsenic, and environmental sources are also possible explanations. The wallpaper theory remains plausible but unproven.

faq.question: How did Victorian society eventually recognize the danger of arsenic pigments?
faq.answer: Physicians began linking mysterious illnesses with green-decorated rooms in the 1860s. William Morris, himself a wallpaper manufacturer whose family owned arsenic mines, eventually removed arsenic greens from his designs. Public awareness campaigns led to gradual abandonment by the 1900s.
